title: Tipping, and whether it should exist

turns.speaker: Kel
turns.text: The card machine asked me for twenty-five per cent at a counter where I carried my own coffee to the table.

turns.speaker: Duncan
turns.text: Tip creep. It's moved from table service to absolutely everything in about five years.

turns.speaker: Rosie
turns.text: Because the screen is turned towards you while somebody watches. That's not a request, it's an audience.

turns.speaker: Kel
turns.text: So abolish it and pay people properly. Some restaurants tried that.

turns.speaker: Duncan
turns.text: And a lot of them went back, because the good servers left. Under tipping a strong server earns more than a flat wage pays.

turns.speaker: Rosie
turns.text: Which is the honest defence of it, and it's also the reason it survives.

turns.speaker: Kel
turns.text: The research on who gets tipped is pretty grim though. Attractiveness, hair colour, race. It's measurable and it's large.

turns.speaker: Kel
turns.text: So it's a wage system with discrimination built into the payment method.

turns.speaker: Duncan
turns.text: That lands. Although a manager setting wages isn't free of that either.

turns.speaker: Rosie
turns.text: No, but a manager can be held to an account. Four hundred customers can't.

turns.speaker: Duncan
turns.text: Fair. The kitchen is the other thing. The person who cooked it usually gets nothing.

turns.speaker: Rosie
turns.text: Which service charges were supposed to fix, and then the pooling rules turned out to be whatever the owner decided.

turns.speaker: Kel
turns.text: That's the part that actually needs legislating, rather than the tipping itself.

points: Tipping prompts have spread from table service to counter service, with high default percentages.
Rosie argues the prompt works through social pressure rather than choice.
Duncan explains attempts to abolish tipping often failed because strong servers earn more under tips than on flat wages.
Kel cites research showing tips vary measurably by attractiveness, hair colour and race, making discrimination part of the payment method.
Rosie distinguishes a manager, who can be held accountable, from hundreds of customers, who cannot.
They agree the clearest target for legislation is how service charges are pooled and whether kitchen staff share, rather than tipping itself.
